test_title: RRB NTPC (UG) CBT-I Official Paper (Held On: 22 Aug, 2025 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: Why is wheat grown in the north-western plains of India?

options.text: Because it lies close to the coastal water bodies
Because it receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon
Because the region has fertile alluvial soil and cool winters
Because the region has red soil with limited annual rainfall

solution:
The correct answer is __**Because the region has fertile alluvial soil and cool winters**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The north-western plains of India are known for their **fertile alluvial soil**, which is deposited by rivers like the **Ganga, Yamuna, Sutlej, and their tributaries**. This soil is rich in nutrients, making it highly suitable for wheat cultivation.
 
• Wheat requires a **cool climate during its growing season**, which the north-western plains provide during winter. The **temperatures range between 10°C to 15°C**, ideal for wheat germination and growth.
 
• The region experiences **adequate irrigation facilities** due to an extensive network of canals, ensuring water availability for wheat crops even during the dry season.
 
• Wheat is a rabi crop, meaning it is sown in winter and harvested in spring. The **low rainfall** during the wheat-growing season in the north-western plains prevents waterlogging, which is detrimental to the crop.
 
• The geographical location provides an advantage, as the plains have a **flat topography**, facilitating large-scale mechanized farming, which is beneficial for wheat cultivation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Alluvial Soil:**

 
 
• Alluvial soil is formed by the deposition of silt, sand, and clay by rivers. It is highly fertile and ideal for growing crops like wheat, rice, sugarcane, and pulses.
 
• The north-western plains have deep alluvial deposits, supporting extensive agricultural activities.
 
 
 
• **Wheat Crop:**
 
 
• Wheat is a **rabi crop**, sown in October-November and harvested in March-April.
 
• It requires a **temperature range of 10°C to 15°C** during germination and 20°C to 25°C during maturity.
 
• Wheat needs around **50-75 cm of annual rainfall**, making the climate of the north-western plains ideal for its growth.
 
• India is the second-largest producer of wheat globally, with major contributions from states like Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Irrigation in North-Western Plains:**
 
 
• The plains have a well-developed **canal irrigation system**, including the Indira Gandhi Canal and Bhakra Nangal Dam system.
 
• This ensures a consistent water supply for wheat cultivation, especially during the dry winter months.
 
 
 
• **Other Crops in the Region:**
 
 
• Besides wheat, the north-western plains are also suitable for growing crops like **rice, sugarcane, mustard, and cotton**.
 
• The availability of fertile soil and water resources makes this region an agricultural hub.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Red Soil and Limited Rainfall:**

 
 
• Red soil, commonly found in southern and eastern India, is not as fertile as alluvial soil and is not ideal for wheat cultivation.
 
• Limited rainfall in regions with red soil also makes it unsuitable for water-intensive crops like wheat.
 
 
 
• **Coastal Proximity:**
 
 
• Coastal regions are not conducive for wheat farming due to **high humidity and saline soil**.
 
• Wheat thrives in inland regions with less humidity and well-drained soil, such as the north-western plains.
 
 
 
• **Rainfall in Monsoon:**
 
 
• Wheat is a rabi crop and does not require heavy monsoon rains, which can damage the crop.
 
• Instead, it requires controlled irrigation during its growing season.
